questions.q: A 35-year-old farmer presents with a painless ulcer on his right hand with a black eschar and significant surrounding edema. He handles animal hides regularly. The most likely causative organism is:
questions.exp: Cutaneous anthrax (malignant pustule) caused by Bacillus anthracis presents with painless ulcer, black eschar and non-pitting edema. Occupational exposure to animal hides is a classic risk factor.

questions.q: A 28-year-old immunocompetent patient develops grouped vesicles on an erythematous base along the T5 dermatome. Two weeks later he develops severe burning pain in the same distribution without any active lesions. The most appropriate management is:
questions.exp: This is postherpetic neuralgia (PHN) following herpes zoster. PHN is defined as pain persisting >3 months after rash onset. Gabapentinoids (gabapentin/pregabalin) and tricyclic antidepressants (amitriptyline) are first-line treatments for neuropathic pain.

questions.q: A 22-year-old sexually active woman presents with painless, firm, indurated ulcer on her vulva with associated rubbery, non-tender inguinal lymphadenopathy. Dark-field microscopy of the exudate would most likely show:
questions.exp: Primary syphilis presents as a painless, indurated chancre with rubbery non-tender lymphadenopathy. Dark-field microscopy of serous exudate reveals Treponema pallidum, a motile spirochete.

questions.q: A 40-year-old male from rural India presents with hypopigmented anaesthetic patches on his trunk and thickened greater auricular nerve. Slit-skin smear shows 3+ bacillary index. As per Ridley-Jopling classification, this patient is best classified as:
questions.exp: High bacillary index (3+), multiple lesions with diffuse distribution, thickened nerves, and anaesthesia suggest Borderline Lepromatous (BL) leprosy on the Ridley-Jopling spectrum. LL typically has BI 5-6+ and TT is paucibacillary with BI 0.

questions.q: A patient on multidrug therapy for lepromatous leprosy develops sudden fever, erythematous tender nodules over his face and extremities, and iridocyclitis. The most appropriate additional treatment is:
questions.exp: This is Type 2 lepra reaction (Erythema Nodosum Leprosum - ENL) characterised by tender erythematous nodules, systemic features and ocular involvement. Thalidomide is the drug of choice for ENL; prednisolone is used when thalidomide is contraindicated (e.g., in women of childbearing age).

questions.q: A 45-year-old woman presents with malar erythema, photosensitivity, oral ulcers, and arthritis for 6 months. ANA is positive (1:640, homogeneous pattern). Which antibody is most specific for this diagnosis?
questions.exp: Anti-dsDNA antibodies are highly specific for Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE) and also correlate with disease activity, particularly lupus nephritis. Anti-histone antibodies are associated with drug-induced lupus; anti-Ro with Sjögren's/neonatal lupus; anti-centromere with limited systemic sclerosis.

questions.q: A 55-year-old woman presents with Raynaud's phenomenon, puffy hands, dysphagia, and progressive skin tightening from distal extremities to the trunk. She has anti-centromere antibodies. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Anti-centromere antibodies are characteristic of limited systemic sclerosis (formerly CREST syndrome). CREST features: Calcinosis, Raynaud's, Esophageal dysmotility, Sclerodactyly, Telangiectasias. Skin involvement is limited to distal extremities and face.

questions.q: A 60-year-old man presents with tense bullae on normal-appearing skin and erythematous plaques. Nikolsky's sign is negative. Histology shows a subepidermal blister with eosinophils. DIF shows linear IgG and C3 deposition at the BMZ. Diagnosis:
questions.exp: Bullous pemphigoid presents in elderly patients with tense blisters (negative Nikolsky's sign), subepidermal blisters with eosinophils on histology, and linear IgG/C3 at BMZ on DIF targeting BP180 and BP230 antigens.

questions.q: A 30-year-old woman presents with painful oral erosions and flaccid bullae on the scalp and chest. Blisters rupture easily leaving raw areas. Nikolsky's sign is positive. Tzanck smear shows acantholytic cells. Which antibody is responsible?
questions.exp: Pemphigus vulgaris is caused by IgG autoantibodies against desmoglein 3 (and desmoglein 1 in mucocutaneous form). It presents with flaccid blisters, oral erosions, positive Nikolsky's sign, and acantholytic cells on Tzanck smear.

questions.q: A 25-year-old patient presents with intensely pruritic vesicles on elbows, knees, and buttocks. He has a history of malabsorption. Skin biopsy shows subepidermal blisters with neutrophils in dermal papillae. DIF shows granular IgA deposits. Best treatment:
questions.exp: Dermatitis herpetiformis presents with intensely pruritic vesicles on extensor surfaces, associated with celiac disease. DIF shows granular IgA in dermal papillae. Treatment is dapsone for itch and strict gluten-free diet as definitive management.

questions.q: A 50-year-old man presents with a pearly, translucent nodule with rolled borders and telangiectasias on his nose. He is a farmer with decades of sun exposure. Diagnosis and first-line treatment:
opts: Squamous cell carcinoma; wide local excision
Basal cell carcinoma; Mohs micrographic surgery
questions.exp: Nodular BCC presents as a pearly papule/nodule with rolled borders, telangiectasias, and central ulceration on sun-exposed skin. Mohs micrographic surgery offers the highest cure rate (>99%) and tissue conservation, especially on the face (H-zone).

questions.q: A 65-year-old immunosuppressed patient develops a rapidly growing, hyperkeratotic, crusted nodule on the lower lip over 6 weeks. Biopsy shows atypical keratinocytes extending into dermis. Which feature confers the highest risk for metastasis?
questions.exp: Perineural invasion is the single most important high-risk feature in squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) associated with metastasis and local recurrence. Other high-risk features include: >2 cm diameter, depth >4 mm, poor differentiation, location on lip/ear, and immunosuppression.

questions.q: A 45-year-old woman presents with an asymmetric, irregularly pigmented lesion (6 mm) on her back with variegated colour (black, brown, red). Dermoscopy shows atypical pigment network and regression areas. Next best step:
opts: Punch biopsy of the darkest area
questions.exp: Suspected melanoma requires excisional biopsy with narrow (1-2 mm) margins to allow accurate Breslow thickness measurement on the entire lesion. Punch or shave biopsies may not sample the deepest part. FNAC is not appropriate for primary diagnosis.

questions.q: A 2-year-old child presents with honey-coloured crusted lesions around the nose and mouth. Gram stain shows gram-positive cocci in clusters. The drug of choice for a localised presentation is:
questions.exp: Impetigo most commonly caused by Staphylococcus aureus (or Streptococcus pyogenes) presents with honey-coloured crusts. For localised disease, topical mupirocin (or retapamulin) is preferred over systemic antibiotics. Fusidic acid is also topical but resistance is a concern.

questions.q: A 30-year-old HIV-positive man (CD4 200 cells/μL) presents with extensive white plaques on his buccal mucosa that can be scraped off revealing an erythematous base. KOH preparation shows pseudohyphae and budding yeast. First-line treatment:
questions.exp: Oral candidiasis (thrush) in HIV patients with CD4 <200 typically requires systemic therapy. Oral fluconazole is the first-line treatment for oropharyngeal candidiasis in immunocompromised patients due to superior efficacy over topical agents.

questions.q: A 20-year-old college student presents with well-demarcated hypopigmented scaly macules on the chest. Wood's lamp shows yellow-green fluorescence. KOH shows 'spaghetti and meatballs' pattern. Diagnosis:
questions.exp: Tinea versicolor (pityriasis versicolor) caused by Malassezia furfur presents with hypo- or hyperpigmented scaly macules on trunk. KOH shows short hyphae and round spores ('spaghetti and meatballs'). Wood's lamp shows golden-yellow fluorescence.

questions.q: A 35-year-old immunocompetent patient presents with painful grouped vesicles in the perigenital area recurring 4 times this year. What is the most appropriate management strategy?
questions.exp: With ≥6 recurrences/year (or ≥4 recurrences causing significant morbidity), daily suppressive antiviral therapy is recommended. Valacyclovir 500 mg OD reduces recurrence frequency by 70-80% and reduces transmission risk. Episodic therapy is used for infrequent recurrences.

questions.q: A 25-year-old man presents with painless cauliflower-like growths on his genitalia. The lesions are soft and skin-coloured. The most appropriate treatment with the lowest recurrence rate is:
questions.exp: Condyloma acuminata (anogenital warts, HPV 6 & 11) can be treated with various modalities. CO2 laser ablation has the lowest recurrence rate (~10-15%) compared to podophyllotoxin (~38%), TCA (~36%), and imiquimod (~13-19%). Recurrence depends on viral load and immune status.

questions.q: A 28-year-old woman presents with erythematous, well-demarcated plaques with silvery-white scales on her elbows and scalp. Auspitz sign is positive. Histopathology would most likely show:
opts: Regular acanthosis, parakeratosis, Munro microabscesses, and suprapapillary thinning
questions.exp: Psoriasis histopathology shows: regular acanthosis (elongated rete ridges), parakeratosis (retention of nuclei in stratum corneum), Munro microabscesses (neutrophils in stratum corneum), Kogoj's spongiform pustules (in early lesions), and suprapapillary thinning with dilated capillaries.

questions.q: A 40-year-old man with plaque psoriasis involving 30% BSA failed topical treatment and phototherapy. He is started on methotrexate. The most important monitoring parameter is:
opts: Liver biopsy after cumulative dose of 3.5–4 g
Complete blood count weekly for 3 months
questions.exp: Methotrexate causes hepatotoxicity (hepatic fibrosis/cirrhosis) with cumulative dosing. Liver biopsy is recommended after a cumulative dose of 3.5-4 g (UK guidelines) or based on transaminase monitoring (Roenigk criteria). CBC monitoring for myelosuppression is important but typically monthly, not weekly after stabilization.

questions.q: A 16-year-old boy presents with erythematous, excoriated papules and vesicles in the antecubital fossae, neck, and behind the knees since childhood, with associated allergic rhinitis. Serum IgE is markedly elevated. The most reliable diagnostic criterion is:
questions.exp: As per Hanifin and Rajka diagnostic criteria for Atopic Dermatitis, pruritus is the essential (major) criterion — it is the cardinal feature without which the diagnosis cannot be made. Elevated IgE, eosinophilia, and positive SPT are minor criteria.

questions.q: A 55-year-old man presents with an ill-defined erythematous scaly plaque on the lower leg with hyperpigmentation and ulceration near the medial malleolus. There is pitting oedema and varicosities. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Gravitational (stasis) eczema is associated with chronic venous insufficiency presenting with medial ankle eczema, hyperpigmentation (hemosiderin), lipodermatosclerosis, and venous ulceration at the gaiter area. Management includes compression bandaging and emollients.

questions.q: A 30-year-old woman with SLE develops a butterfly-shaped facial rash that spares the nasolabial folds. She is started on hydroxychloroquine. The most important side effect to monitor is:
questions.exp: Hydroxychloroquine can cause irreversible retinal toxicity (bull's eye maculopathy) with cumulative dosing. Annual ophthalmologic screening with automated visual fields and OCT is recommended after 5 years of use (or earlier if risk factors present). Cardiomyopathy is rare.

questions.q: A 70-year-old man presents with palpable purpura on both lower extremities, haematuria, and arthralgia. Skin biopsy shows leukocytoclastic vasculitis (LCV) with IgA deposits on DIF. The underlying diagnosis is:
questions.exp: IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schönlein Purpura) is characterised by IgA-dominant immune deposits in vessel walls, palpable purpura (lower extremities), arthralgia, renal involvement (IgA nephropathy), and abdominal pain. DIF showing IgA deposits in skin vessels is pathognomonic.

questions.q: A 35-year-old man presents with localised patches of complete depigmentation on the dorsum of hands and around the mouth, with leukotrichia. Wood's lamp examination shows chalk-white fluorescence. The most appropriate treatment for stable, localised vitiligo is:
questions.exp: For stable, localised vitiligo, topical tacrolimus (calcineurin inhibitor) is preferred, especially on the face and in children, due to its efficacy and safety profile without skin atrophy risk. Narrowband UVB is first-line for widespread disease. Oral PUVA has higher side effects.

questions.q: A 48-year-old woman presents with multiple comedones (open and closed), inflammatory papules and pustules, and nodules on her cheeks and forehead. She was prescribed isotretinoin. Which monitoring is essential before and during treatment?
questions.exp: Isotretinoin is a potent teratogen (Category X). iPLEDGE/mandatory pregnancy prevention program requires two negative pregnancy tests before starting, monthly tests during treatment, and reliable contraception. Serum lipids (triglycerides) and liver function tests are also monitored.

questions.q: A 52-year-old woman presents with chronic pruritic, violaceous, flat-topped polygonal papules on the flexor surface of the wrists. Biopsy shows a 'sawtooth' pattern of rete ridges, band-like lymphocytic infiltrate at the DEJ, and colloid bodies. The oral equivalent shows a lacy white pattern. Diagnosis:
questions.exp: Lichen planus — the 5 Ps: Pruritic, Purple, Polygonal, Planar (flat-topped) Papules. Histology: sawtooth rete ridges, band-like lymphocytic infiltrate at DEJ, Max Joseph spaces, colloid (civatte) bodies. Wickham's striae (lacy white) on oral mucosa.

questions.q: A 60-year-old male farmer presents with verrucous plaques on the lower leg with suppurating sinuses discharging black granules. Culture on Sabouraud's dextrose agar grows slow-growing dark colonies. Diagnosis and treatment of choice:
questions.exp: Mycetoma (Madura foot) presents with triad of: tumefaction, sinuses, and granule discharge. Black granules suggest eumycetoma (fungal, e.g., Madurella mycetomatis). Treatment: itraconazole/voriconazole with surgical debulking. Chromoblastomycosis shows sclerotic bodies on histology without grain discharge.

questions.q: A 25-year-old nurse presents with erythema, vesicles, and weeping on the dorsum of both hands after starting work with latex gloves and disinfectants. Patch testing shows positive reaction to thiuram at 48 and 72 hours. The type of hypersensitivity involved is:
questions.exp: Allergic contact dermatitis is a Type IV (delayed-type) hypersensitivity reaction mediated by sensitized T lymphocytes. Patch testing is the gold standard diagnostic test, reading at 48h and 72-96h. Irritant contact dermatitis does not require sensitization and is not immune-mediated.

questions.q: A 45-year-old HIV-positive man (CD4 50 cells/μL) develops rapidly progressive, extensive molluscum contagiosum lesions (>100) with giant forms on the face. The most effective management strategy is:
questions.exp: In severely immunocompromised HIV patients (CD4 <100), molluscum contagiosum becomes extensive and giant. The most effective treatment is immune reconstitution through cART, which allows the immune system to clear the virus. Local destructive therapies are adjuncts but unsustainable for hundreds of lesions.
